To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the nonpeptide and the peptide nociceptor populations are distinct in their transsynaptic connections and that the major ascending pathways of the nonpeptides are directed to motor and limbic regions of the basal ganglia, hypothalamus and amygdala, whereas the peptides project primarily to the thalamus and to the parabrachial region.

the major ascending circuits of nonpeptide nocicetors arise from lamina II interneurons and that they target the amygdala and hypothalamus, the bed nucleus of the striat terminalis, and the globus pallidas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular and circuitry mechanisms of nociception.
the neural basis of pain, which has been a central focus in neuroscience for many years.
the neurobiological underpinnings of chronic pain and the mechanisms that underlie the development and maintenance of pain hypersensitivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the nociceptive pathways arising from the nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors differ in their central projections, and that these differences may be related to the differential expression of the Na(V)1,8 and TRPV1 channels.
there is a parallel pain pathway, but the pain pathway is not the same as the nociceptive pathway.
the nonpeptide pathway is a major pathway for pain transmission, and it is a pathway that is independent of the peptide pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the non-peptide nociceptor class engages a parallel "pain" pathway that targets limbic and motor circuits and is independent of the lamina I "pain" pathway.

the nonpeptide and peptide classes of nociceptor are differentially connected to the central nervous system and that these connections are consistent with the idea that these classes of nociceptive neuron are differentially engaged in different aspects of pain processing.
the nonpeptide and the peptide nociceptor subpopulations are not only anatomically distinct but also engage different central circuits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different classes of nociceptor, and by implication, different classes of pain, engage different ascending pathways and thus may have different therapeutic targets.

there is a major difference in the central circuits engaged by the two classes of nociceptor, and that this difference is likely to reflect differences in the nature of the sensory inputs that these two classes of nocieptor convey.
there are at least two parallel nociceptive pathways, one for peptides and one for nonpeptides.
